::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🎯 Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

-   Explain what a bioinformatician does, and what they need from you
-   Describe the three main sequencing technologies and what each is good for
-   Say what a FASTQ, BAM, VCF, and count matrix each contain — without opening one
-   Explain why the choice of reference genome and annotation changes results
-   Name the major public omics repositories and what lives in each
-   Recognize the three statistical traps that ruin most omics analyses
-   Have a productive design conversation *before* you send samples for sequencing
:::

> 🤔 **Motivating question**
>
> Your samples came back. There is a link to 200 GB of data on a server you have never logged into. What happens now?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. What Bioinformatics Is 👩‍💻 {#w1-s1}

## 1) Bio + Information {#w1-s1-1}

A compound word, and both halves matter.

-   **Bio** ➡️ human samples, cells, tissues — with phenotypes attached
-   **Information** ➡️ data, usually omics data, usually a very large table

![Bioinformatics sits at the intersection of biology, computer science, and statistics — and spans the whole path from sample to interpretation.](/assets/img/w1/bioinformatics.png){fig-align="center"}

**The job** — turn the second into a statement about the first.

**The difficulty** — the translation is *lossy in both directions*:

-   A tumour ➡️ a matrix of numbers
-   A matrix of numbers ➡️ a claim about a tumour

Most of this course is about where information leaks out at each step.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2) Three neighbouring fields {#w1-s1-2}

Often used interchangeably. Different jobs.

| Field | Central question | Typical output |
|--------------------|------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Bioinformatics** | How do I get from raw data to an interpretable measurement? | Processed matrices, variant calls, annotated gene lists |
| **Computational biology** | Can I build a model that explains or predicts biology? | Simulations, predictive models, mechanistic theory |
| **Biostatistics** | Given this design, what can I legitimately conclude? | Estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, study designs |

In practice one person does all three. The distinction matters when deciding **who to ask**:

-   "My aligner is throwing away 40% of reads" → bioinformatics
-   "Is n = 3 enough?" → biostatistics, and it should have been asked months earlier

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The most useful thing you will learn this semester

Not how to run anything.

Recognizing **which of those three questions you are actually asking** — because asking the wrong specialist wastes months.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3) Wet lab ➡️ dry lab {#w1-s1-3}

You already have the right reflexes. A beautiful Western blot prompts: what was the loading control? how many biological replicates? was the exposure saturated?

Same reflexes, different artifacts:

| Wet lab habit | Dry lab equivalent |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Loading control | Normalization (W4) |
| Antibody validation | Reference database / annotation choice (W1, W6) |
| Blinding and randomization | Batch design and randomized sample layout (W1) |
| Technical vs. biological replicate | The same distinction, more consequential (W4) |
| "It worked once" | A finding that does not replicate in a second cohort |

**The failure mode unique to computation** — the analysis always produces an answer.

-   Failed PCR → an empty gel. Obvious
-   Failed RNA-seq analysis → a tidy table of 847 genes, sorted by p-value. **Nothing about its appearance tells you it is wrong**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4) The generic omics workflow 🗺️ {#w1-s1-4}

The omics layers of the next six weeks, organized by the central dogma — each with its own characteristic question.

![W2 works on the genome, W3 on its regulatory state, W4–W5 on the transcriptome, W6 on the proteome. W7 asks the same questions of a second genome — the microbiome.](/assets/img/w1/central_dogma.png){fig-align="center"}

Every analysis in this course — genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metagenomics — follows the same five stages.

```         
① Quality control     → is this data usable at all?
② Alignment /          → where did each measurement come from,
   quantification         and how much of it is there?
③ Normalization       → make samples comparable to each other
④ Statistical testing → which differences are larger than noise?
⑤ Interpretation      → what does that mean biologically?
```

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## This is the map for the whole course

Every week from W2 onward: ask where in these five stages you are. The technologies differ enormously; the stages barely change.

The stages are also where the errors live — and they are **not equally dangerous**:

-   Stage ① ② errors → **loud**. The pipeline crashes, or the numbers are absurd
-   Stage ③ ④ errors → **quiet**. These are the ones that reach publication
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Sequencing and Data 🧪 {#w1-s2}

## 1) Sequencing technologies in one hour {#w1-s2-1}

Nearly all omics data here comes from **sequencing DNA** — even when the question is about RNA, chromatin, or protein binding. The trick that made omics possible: convert every molecular question into "count the DNA fragments."

The other enabler was economics — cost per genome fell faster than Moore's law, from \~\$100 million in 2001 to a few hundred dollars today.

![Cost per human genome. The discontinuity around 2007–2008 is the arrival of massively parallel short-read sequencing. Source: NHGRI.](/assets/img/w1/cost_per_genome.jpg){fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why this graph matters for you

-   **Then** — the bottleneck was *generating* data
-   **Now** — the bottleneck is *interpreting* it, and increasingly, having a design worth interpreting

That shift is the entire reason this course exists.
:::

### ① Sanger sequencing {#w1-s2-1-1}

> chain termination with fluorescently labelled ddNTPs

-   The original method; still the clinical gold standard for confirming a single variant
-   One reaction = one template, up to \~800–1,000 bases
-   Very high per-base accuracy

![Sanger sequencing. A ddNTP lacks the 3′-OH needed for the next phosphodiester bond, so incorporation terminates the chain. A ladder of fragments of every length, each labelled by its terminal base, reads out the sequence.](/assets/img/w1/sanger_seq.png){fig-align="center"}

⚠️ The limitation is **throughput, not quality**. One gene is trivial. One genome took thirteen years and \~\$3 billion.

### ② Short-read sequencing (Illumina) {#w1-s2-1-2}

> massively parallel sequencing by synthesis

**The key idea — parallelism.** Not one molecule read well, but hundreds of millions read simultaneously, each moderately well.

The workflow:

-   **Library preparation** — fragment the DNA, ligate adapters to both ends
-   **Cluster generation** — each fragment amplified in place on a flow cell
-   **Sequencing by synthesis** — one fluorescent, reversibly terminated base per cycle: add, image, unblock; repeat 50–300×

![Left: library preparation — fragmentation, adapter ligation, denaturation. Right: bridge amplification on the flow cell, which turns one molecule into a cluster bright enough to image.](/assets/img/w1/library_prep.png){fig-align="center"}

##### The library molecule

Everything entering the sequencer: **adapter + insert + adapter**. Each component has a job.

![P5/P7 bind the flow cell. Rd1/Rd2 SP are the sequencing primer binding sites. Index1/Index2 identify the sample.](/assets/img/w1/ngs_adapter.png){fig-align="center" width="700"}

Two features matter for interpretation:

-   **Index (barcode)** — 6–12 nt, identifies the sample
    -   Enables *multiplexing*: many samples in one lane, demultiplexed afterwards
    -   ⚠️ Also where sample swaps and **index hopping** happen — reads assigned to the wrong sample. Dual indexing exists because single indexing was not reliable enough
-   **Single-end vs. paired-end** — reading the fragment from one end or both

![Single-end gives one read per fragment; paired-end gives two, with a known approximate distance between them. That distance is what lets an aligner place reads confidently in repetitive regions and detect splice junctions and rearrangements.](/assets/img/w1/paired_end.png){fig-align="center"}

-   Paired-end costs more → better alignment in repeats, plus structural rearrangements and splice junctions (🔗 W4)
-   Typical output today: 2 × 150 bp, per-base error \~0.1%
-   ⚠️ **Read length is the fundamental limit** — 150 bases is shorter than most repeats, most structural variants, and most full-length transcripts

### ③ Long-read sequencing (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) {#w1-s2-1-3}

> read the whole molecule, accept more errors per base

-   **PacBio HiFi** — circular template read repeatedly, consensus taken. \~15–25 kb reads, accuracy comparable to short reads
-   **Oxford Nanopore** — single strand threaded through a protein pore, ionic current decoded
    -   Reads can exceed a megabase
    -   Raw accuracy below Illumina, though modern chemistries have narrowed the gap considerably
    -   Detects base modifications (e.g. DNA methylation) directly, without bisulfite conversion (🔗 W3)

### ④ The trade-off triangle {#w1-s2-1-4}

Read length, per-base accuracy, cost per base — you cannot maximize all three. Every platform picks a corner.

|   | Read length | Accuracy | Cost / Gb | Best for |
|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|---------------------|
| **Sanger** | \~800 bp | Very high | Very high | Confirming a single variant |
| **Illumina** | 50–300 bp | High | Low | Counting: RNA-seq, ChIP, WGS/WES at scale |
| **PacBio HiFi** | 15–25 kb | High | Moderate | Assembly, structural variants, phasing |
| **Nanopore** | up to Mb | Moderate | Moderate | Ultra-long spans, direct modification calling, portability |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The question to ask about any dataset

Not "which platform?" but **"is the read long enough to answer my question?"**

-   Variant in a segmental duplication? → 150 bp reads will not save you
-   Transcript with ten isoforms differing at the 3′ end? → same

No amount of depth fixes a read-length problem.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2) The shape of biological data {#w1-s2-2}

You will probably never open these files by hand — but you will read methods sections that mention them, and reviewers will ask.

What matters: **what each format holds, and what it has already thrown away.**

### ① FASTQ — the raw read {#w1-s2-2-1}

Four lines per read, tens of millions of reads per sample.

```         
@SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51           ← read ID
GCCTTGGTGGTGAAATGGTAGACTGGAATTCTCGGGTGCC   ← sequence
+SRR21484222.626.1 626 length=51           ← description
F:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFF   ← base quality (Phred)
```

-   **Knows** — the sequence, and the machine's confidence in each base
-   **Does not know** — where in the genome the read came from. That information does not exist yet

##### Phred quality score

$$Q = -10 \log_{10} P$$

where $P$ = probability that the base call is wrong.

| Phred score | Error rate  | Base call accuracy |
|-------------|-------------|--------------------|
| 10          | 1 in 10     | 90%                |
| 20          | 1 in 100    | 99%                |
| 30          | 1 in 1,000  | 99.9%              |
| 40          | 1 in 10,000 | 99.99%             |

Q30 = the conventional benchmark. "\>80% of bases above Q30" is the sort of line you will see in a facility report.

### ② BAM — reads placed on a genome {#w1-s2-2-2}

Every read + the coordinate the aligner assigned + a **mapping quality** for that assignment.

⚠️ **Alignment is inference, not observation.**

-   A read from a repetitive region could plausibly come from several places
-   The aligner picks one and lowers the mapping quality to say so
-   Analyses that ignore mapping quality silently accept a lot of wrong placements

BAM is where read-level information ends for most projects — large (tens of GB per WGS sample), and everything downstream is a summary of it.

### ③ VCF — differences from a reference {#w1-s2-2-3}

Positions where your sample differs from the reference, with genotype and quality. Everything shared with the reference is implicit and absent.

⚠️ **A VCF is a diff, not a genome.**

-   A region that could not be aligned produces no variants
-   That looks identical to a region with no variants
-   **Absence of a call ≠ a call of absence**

### ④ Count matrix — where most analyses actually begin {#w1-s2-2-4}

Features (genes, peaks, proteins, taxa) in rows × samples in columns, one number per cell.

-   What public repositories distribute, and what statistical methods consume
-   Also the point of **maximum information loss** — every read, alignment, and quality score compressed into one integer per gene per sample

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## What the count matrix has already decided for you

By the time it reaches you, someone has already chosen:

-   Reference genome build
-   Annotation version
-   Aligner
-   Quantification method
-   Rules for multi-mapping reads

All invisible in the matrix. All capable of changing your results substantially.

→ Download a matrix from GEO, and **the original paper's methods section is part of your methods section.**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3) The reference genome {#w1-s2-3}

### ① GRCh38 and T2T-CHM13 {#w1-s2-3-1}

Not a person's genome — a mosaic from several donors, curated over two decades. An idealized coordinate system everyone agrees to use.

-   **GRCh38** (2013) — the workhorse. Still the default for most clinical and population resources, largely because enormous datasets are already mapped to it
-   **T2T-CHM13** (2022) — the first genuinely complete assembly: centromeres, acrocentric short arms, and other GRCh38 gaps. Adds \~200 Mb of previously unmapped sequence
-   **Pangenome references** — a graph of many haplotypes rather than one linear sequence. Where the field is heading; not yet the default

⚠️ **Coordinates are not interchangeable between builds.**

-   A position in GRCh37 (hg19) is a different position in GRCh38
-   "Liftover" is routine but lossy
-   Mixing builds is one of the commonest sources of nonsense results in student projects

### ② Annotation: where the genes are {#w1-s2-3-2}

-   **Reference sequence** — what the bases are
-   **Annotation** — which stretches are genes, exons, transcripts, regulatory elements

Separate files, separately versioned, and they disagree with each other.

-   **GENCODE** — comprehensive; used by ENCODE and GTEx. Includes many lncRNAs and predicted transcripts
-   **RefSeq** — NCBI's conservative, manually curated set. Standard in clinical reporting

\~20,000 protein-coding genes — a remarkably stable number. But *transcript* counts differ by tens of thousands between sources and versions.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Annotation version is a hidden variable

Same FASTQ files + different GENCODE release →

-   different gene counts
-   different library totals
-   → different normalization factors
-   → different DE results

Usually modest differences. Occasionally not.

**Report the build *and* the annotation version. Every time.**
:::

### ③ Reference bias {#w1-s2-3-3}

Everything is measured relative to one sequence → anything poorly represented in that sequence is systematically under-detected.

-   **Divergent haplotypes** — reads from non-European-ancestry individuals map slightly worse to a reference built mostly from European donors → subtle allele-frequency and coverage biases (🔗 W2)
-   **Highly polymorphic loci** — HLA is the classic case; standard alignment badly misrepresents it
-   **Repetitive and duplicated regions** — reads map ambiguously or not at all
-   **Sequence absent from the reference** — undetectable by definition

🗺️ First appearance of a thread running through the whole course: **reference bias**.

-   W3 → chromatin atlases
-   W4 → annotation versions
-   W6 → the protein search database
-   W7 → the 16S taxonomy database

Same problem, different name.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. Where the Data Lives 🗄️ {#w1-s3}

More usable public omics data exists than any lab could generate. For many questions the fastest path to an answer is **reanalysis, not a new experiment**.

## 1) Open repositories {#w1-s3-1}

| Resource | Contents | Access |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------|----------------|
| **GEO** (NCBI) | Processed matrices + metadata, all assay types | Open |
| **SRA** (NCBI) | Raw reads (FASTQ) | Open |
| **ENA** (EMBL-EBI) | Raw reads, European mirror of SRA | Open |
| **ArrayExpress / BioStudies** | Functional genomics experiments | Open |
| **PRIDE** | Mass spectrometry proteomics (🔗 W6) | Open |
| **MetaboLights** | Metabolomics | Open |

## 2) Controlled access {#w1-s3-2}

Individual-level human genotype data is identifying → cannot be posted openly. Access requires an application describing intended use.

| Resource | Contents | Access |
|----------------|---------------------------------------|----------------|
| **dbGaP** | US individual-level genotype/phenotype | Application |
| **EGA** | European equivalent | Application |
| **UK Biobank** | \~500,000 participants: genotype, imaging, EHR linkage | Application + fee |
| **All of Us** | US diversity-focused cohort | Application |

💡 Applications take **weeks to months**. Start at the *proposal* stage, not when you are ready to analyze.

## 3) Consortium atlases {#w1-s3-3}

Reference resources rather than experiments — you look things up in them.

| Resource | What it gives you | Appears in |
|--------------------------|------------------------------|----------------|
| **GTEx** | Normal-tissue expression across \~54 tissues; eQTLs | W2, W4 |
| **ENCODE / Roadmap** | Regulatory element and chromatin maps across cell types | W3 |
| **TCGA** | Multi-omics across 33 cancer types, with clinical follow-up | W2, W4 |
| **Human Cell Atlas / Tabula Sapiens** | Single-cell reference atlases | W5 |
| **1000 Genomes / gnomAD** | Population allele frequencies | W2 |
| **Human Protein Atlas** | Protein expression and localization | W6 |

## 4) 💡 What makes a public dataset worth reanalyzing {#w1-s3-4}

Not all deposited data is usable. Check before committing a semester to a GEO accession:

-   ✅ **Sample size** — n \> 30 per group for most bulk questions. Small studies are underpowered no matter how clean
-   ✅ **Clear design** — unambiguous case vs. control, or a paired design (stronger: within-patient variation is controlled statistically)
-   ✅ **Rich metadata** — age, sex, batch, tissue, treatment. A matrix without covariates cannot be corrected for confounding
-   ✅ **Raw data available** — reprocessing with your own annotation needs the FASTQs, not just the matrix
-   ⚠️ **Batch structure recoverable** — all cases in one batch and all controls in another → unsalvageable. This is common. Check first

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Statistics You Cannot Avoid 📊 {#w1-s4}

Omics data is **high-dimensional**: large *p* (features), small *n* (samples). Twenty thousand genes, twelve patients. Every intuition built on the opposite ratio breaks here.

## 1) What a p-value does and does not say {#w1-s4-1}

**Is** — the probability of data at least this extreme *if the null hypothesis were true*. That is all.

**Is not** —

-   the probability that the null hypothesis is true
-   the probability that your finding will replicate
-   a measure of effect size
-   any statement about biological importance

Two illustrations:

-   n = 200 per group → a 3% expression difference can reach p \< 0.001 and mean nothing
-   n = 3 → a genuine two-fold change can fail to reach significance

→ **Always read the effect size alongside the p-value.**

## 2) Multiple testing {#w1-s4-2}

-   One gene at α = 0.05 → 5% chance of a false positive
-   20,000 genes, no real signal at all → **\~1,000 false positives expected**

Two corrections dominate:

| Method | Controls | Behaviour | Use when |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Bonferroni** | Family-wise error rate — P(≥1 false positive) | Very conservative | You need near-certainty about every hit (e.g. GWAS, 🔗 W2) |
| **Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR)** | Expected *proportion* of false positives among hits | Much more permissive | Screening / discovery (e.g. RNA-seq, 🔗 W4) |

FDR is the omics default — the goal is usually a *ranked candidate list* for follow-up, not individually certain claims.

"FDR \< 0.05" = about 5% of the genes on this list are expected to be false.

-   Acceptable bargain when the next step is **validation**
-   Unacceptable when the next step is a **clinical decision**

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## The correction cannot be applied after the fact

-   Tested 20,000 genes, found one interesting result, reported only that one with an uncorrected p-value? → you have not avoided the multiple testing problem, you have **hidden** it
-   Tried six normalization methods and reported the one with the nicest volcano plot? → also multiple testing, and **no correction exists for it**
:::

## 3) Batch effects and confounding ⚠️ {#w1-s4-3}

**Batch effect** — systematic technical variation between groups of samples processed together: different days, reagent lots, flow cells, technicians, extraction kits.

In omics it is routinely **larger than the biological effect you are looking for**.

Batch effects are annoying but survivable. **Confounding is fatal:**

```         
Recoverable:   Batch 1 = 5 cases + 5 controls
               Batch 2 = 5 cases + 5 controls
               → batch can be modelled and removed

Unrecoverable: Batch 1 = 10 cases
               Batch 2 = 10 controls
               → batch and disease are the same variable
                 no statistical method can separate them
```

In the second case:

-   every method that removes the batch effect also removes your signal
-   every method that preserves the signal preserves the artifact
-   → the experiment cannot be rescued by analysis. It has to be redesigned

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Randomize your sample layout

Costs nothing. Prevents the single most common unrecoverable error in omics studies.

When laying samples on a plate or submitting for sequencing, **distribute conditions evenly across every technical grouping** — plate, row, run, day, operator.

If you take one practical thing from this chapter, take this one.
:::

## 4) Power, effect size, and n {#w1-s4-4}

**Statistical power** — the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size.

Depends on: effect size · variability · n · and in omics, the multiple testing burden (the threshold is far stricter than 0.05).

Rough orientation, not rules:

-   **Bulk RNA-seq** — n = 3 detects only large, consistent changes. n = 6–10 is a working minimum for human tissue. n \> 20 for clinically heterogeneous phenotypes
-   **GWAS** — thousands to hundreds of thousands; individual variant effects are tiny (🔗 W2)
-   **Single-cell** — the relevant n is the number of *donors*, not cells. Three donors is three, whether you sequenced 300 cells or 300,000 (🔗 W5)

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Underpowered studies are worse than no study

They do not simply fail to find things. What they *do* find is:

-   enriched for false positives
-   systematically **inflated in effect size** — only the largest apparent effects survive the significance filter

→ why small pilot studies so often fail to replicate at their reported effect size.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Reproducibility and Study Design ♻️ {#w1-s5}

## 1) Why the same data gives different answers {#w1-s5-1}

Identical FASTQ files → two competent analysts → two different gene lists. Overlap is usually good, rarely complete.

The divergence accumulates from individually reasonable choices:

-   Reference build and annotation version
-   Aligner and its parameters
-   Handling of multi-mapping reads
-   Filtering thresholds for low-expression features
-   Normalization method
-   The statistical model, and which covariates it includes
-   Significance and effect-size thresholds

None of these is *wrong*. But there are enough of them that a determined analyst can reach almost any conclusion — usually without realizing it, by stopping when the result looks biologically sensible.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The defense

-   Decide the analysis plan **before** seeing the results
-   Write it down
-   Explore if you must — but label exploratory findings as exploratory

Standard practice in clinical trials for exactly this reason. Omics is at least as vulnerable.
:::

## 2) What a good methods section contains {#w1-s5-2}

You will write these, and you will review them.

-   ✅ Reference build **and** annotation version, with release numbers
-   ✅ Every tool with its version number
-   ✅ Non-default parameters
-   ✅ Filtering criteria — how many features and samples removed, and why
-   ✅ The full statistical model, including covariates
-   ✅ Multiple testing correction method and threshold
-   ✅ Accession numbers for data, and a link to analysis code

❌ "Data were analyzed using standard pipelines" is not a methods section. You will see it in print constantly.

## 3) 🗣️ The conversation to have before you sequence {#w1-s5-3}

The highest-value section of this chapter. **Most analysis problems are design problems that became visible too late.**

Agree on these before samples leave your bench:

| Question | Why it matters |
|----------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| **What is the comparison?** | Determines the whole design. "Let's see what's different" is not a comparison |
| **How many biological replicates?** | The single biggest determinant of what you can detect |
| **What is the unit of replication?** | Patients? Mice? Wells? Cells? This is where n is usually overstated |
| **What covariates will we need?** | Age, sex, batch, RIN, cell composition. Collect them now; you cannot add them later |
| **How will samples be laid out?** | Randomize across batches. Non-negotiable |
| **What are the technical constraints?** | Read length, depth, single vs. paired-end — driven by the question, not the price list |
| **Is there a validation plan?** | An orthogonal assay, or an independent cohort. Reviewers will ask |

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Ask your analyst one question

**"Given this design, what would I be able to conclude if the experiment works perfectly?"**

If the honest answer is "not much" — you have just saved yourself a year, before spending anything.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 📝 Summary

-   Bioinformatics converts samples into data and back again; information is lost in both directions
-   Nearly every omics assay reduces to **counting DNA fragments** — technologies differ mainly in read length, accuracy, and cost
-   FASTQ ➡️ BAM ➡️ VCF / count matrix = increasing summarization. Each step discards information and embeds decisions
-   All analyses follow five stages: **QC ➡️ quantification ➡️ normalization ➡️ testing ➡️ interpretation**. Stages ③ ④ hide the dangerous errors
-   The reference genome and its annotation are choices, not facts — and they bias results systematically
-   Public data is abundant; the limiting factor is metadata quality and batch structure, not volume
-   Large *p*, small *n* → multiple testing is unavoidable. FDR for discovery, Bonferroni when certainty matters
-   ⚠️ **Batch confounded with condition cannot be fixed by any analysis.** Randomize sample layout
-   The most valuable thing a bioinformatician does happens **before** sequencing

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🔑 Key terms

| Term | One-line meaning |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Read | One sequenced fragment |
| Phred score | Log-scaled probability that a base call is wrong |
| Coverage / depth | Average number of reads over each position |
| Alignment / mapping | Inferring where a read came from in the genome |
| Mapping quality | Confidence in that inference |
| Multiplexing | Pooling barcoded samples in one sequencing run |
| Reference genome | Agreed coordinate system for the species |
| Annotation | Where genes, exons, and elements sit on that system |
| Reference bias | Systematic under-detection of anything unlike the reference |
| Count matrix | Features × samples table of measurements |
| Batch effect | Systematic technical variation between processing groups |
| Confounding | Two variables varying together, statistically inseparable |
| FDR | Expected proportion of false positives among significant results |
| Statistical power | Probability of detecting a real effect of a given size |
